issues.legal_issue: A court’s recorded permission and finding that a compromise benefits a minor can satisfy the requirement for judicial sanction without a prescribed form of certificate.
material_facts: A minor was a party to a partition suit in which the parties proposed a compromise.
The court’s order stated that permission to compromise was granted because the compromise was for the minors’ benefit.
issues.conclusion: The court’s order sufficiently recorded its permission and satisfaction that the compromise benefited the minors; the objection to the form or sufficiency of the sanction failed.
issues.legal_principle: Order 32, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires the court to sanction a compromise affecting a minor and to be satisfied that it is for the minor’s benefit, but prescribes no set form for recording that satisfaction.

predicates.minor_party_in_civil_suit: A minor was a party to the civil suit in which a compromise was proposed.
predicates.court_granted_compromise_permission: The court granted permission for the compromise.
predicates.court_recorded_benefit_finding: The court recorded that the compromise was for the minor’s benefit.

issues.definition: When a minor is a party to a civil suit and the court grants permission while recording that the compromise benefits the minor, the court’s sanction is sufficient.

issues.legal_issue: A guardian need not obtain the court’s sanction before beginning negotiations for a compromise affecting a minor if the court later sanctions the compromise and finds it beneficial to the minor.
material_facts: The guardian and the other parties had reached a compromise before the court granted permission.
The court then granted permission, recording that the compromise was for the minors’ benefit, and a decree followed on that basis.
issues.conclusion: The compromise and decree were not invalid merely because the guardian had not obtained the court’s sanction before beginning negotiations or reaching agreement.
issues.legal_principle: Order 32, rule 7, read as a whole, does not require advance permission before negotiations begin. Under sub-rule (2), an agreement made without the required sanction is not a nullity but is voidable at the minor’s option; where the court sanctions the compromise and finds it beneficial, the decree may bind the minor. The Court disapproved the contrary view in Awadhesh Prasad Missir v. Widow of Tribeni Prasad Missir.

rule.if: minor_party_in_civil_suit and guardian_agreed_before_permission and court_sanctioned_compromise and court_found_compromise_beneficial

predicates.minor_party_in_civil_suit: A minor was a party to the civil suit in which the compromise was made.
predicates.guardian_agreed_before_permission: The guardian reached agreement before obtaining the court’s permission.
predicates.court_sanctioned_compromise: The court later sanctioned the compromise.
predicates.court_found_compromise_beneficial: The court found that the compromise was for the minor’s benefit.

issues.definition: When a guardian reaches agreement before permission but the court later sanctions a beneficial compromise involving a minor, the compromise can bind the minor.

issues.legal_issue: A minor properly represented in a court decree partitioning family property cannot set aside the decree merely because the division was unfair.
material_facts: A minor was a party to a partition suit and was represented before the court by a guardian.
The court sanctioned the compromise on which the partition decree was based.
The minor’s challenge asserted that the partition was unfair, but fraud or negligence by the guardian was not established.
issues.conclusion: The decree was binding on the minor despite alleged unfairness; the rule allowing a minor to challenge an unfair partition does not apply to a decree in a suit where the minor was properly represented, absent fraud or negligence by the guardian.
issues.legal_principle: The rule in Mulla’s Hindu Law, drawing on Balkishen Das v. Ram Narain Sahu, that a minor may set aside an unfair partition applies to partitions not effected by a decree of a competent court. A decree binds a properly represented minor as it binds adult parties unless fraud or negligence by the next friend or guardian ad litem is shown.

rule.if: partition_suit_decree and minor_properly_represented and division_unfair and not guardian_fraud_or_negligence

predicates.partition_suit_decree: A court decree determined a partition of family property in a partition suit.
predicates.minor_properly_represented: A minor party was properly represented before the court by a next friend or guardian.
predicates.division_unfair: The minor alleges or shows that the division was unfair.
predicates.guardian_fraud_or_negligence: The minor establishes fraud or negligence by the next friend or guardian.

issues.definition: If a partition decree was made in a suit where the minor was properly represented, unfairness alone does not displace the decree when guardian fraud or negligence is absent.

issues.legal_issue: Claims of fraud, undue influence, or coercion require separate pleading of the relevant ground and full particulars, and general allegations are insufficient.
material_facts: The plaintiffs alleged that a family member pressured their father into a compromise and used coercion and undue influence.
The allegations did not separately plead coercion and undue influence or provide particulars of the alleged threat, including its nature, time, place, circumstances, or the person who made it.
The evidence did not establish the alleged threat or undue influence, and the father’s conduct after the compromise was inconsistent with the allegations.
issues.conclusion: The allegations and evidence did not establish coercion or undue influence, so those grounds for setting aside the compromise failed.
issues.legal_principle: Order 6, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires full particulars when fraud, undue influence, or coercion is pleaded. These are distinct legal grounds that must be separately pleaded; general allegations are insufficient, and the case must be decided on the particulars pleaded.

predicates.civil_claim_alleges_coercion_or_undue_in: A party to a civil case alleges that coercion or undue influence affected an agreement or compromise.
predicates.grounds_not_separately_pleaded: The party does not plead coercion and undue influence as separate grounds.
predicates.material_particulars_missing: The pleading omits material particulars of the alleged conduct.

issues.definition: When a civil claim alleging coercion or undue influence does not separately plead the grounds and omits material particulars, the claim fails.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot direct partition of disputed properties without trying the relevant issue or receiving evidence on whether those properties are subject to partition.
material_facts: The trial court directed partition of properties that the opposing party disputed were subject to partition.
The relevant issue was not tried and no evidence was led on it.
issues.conclusion: The trial court’s direction to partition those properties could not be upheld.
issues.legal_principle: A court cannot decree partition of properties whose status as partitionable property is disputed without trying that dispute and considering evidence.

predicates.civil_suit_seeking_partition: A civil suit seeks partition of property.
predicates.property_partitionability_disputed: A party disputes whether the property is subject to partition.
predicates.issue_not_tried_and_no_evidence: The court neither tried the disputed issue nor received evidence on it.

issues.definition: In a partition suit, a direction concerning disputed property cannot stand when the question whether it is partitionable was neither tried nor supported by evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A court may leave a claimed right to partition for determination in an earlier pending suit between the same parties seeking the same relief, without deciding that right in the later suit.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought to challenge an earlier compromise decree and also asserted a right to partition property said to have been left undivided.
An earlier suit between the same parties seeking partition of that property was already pending.
The court dismissed the present suit while expressly leaving the plaintiffs’ right to seek partition for determination in the pending suit.
issues.conclusion: The court did not adjudicate the right to partition the properties said to have been omitted from the compromise; that matter was left for the pending suit.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered it more convenient and proper to have the partition questions determined in the previously instituted suit between the same parties for the same relief, and expressly preserved the right to pursue partition there.

predicates.later_civil_suit_seeks_partition_relief: A later civil suit seeks partition relief.
predicates.earlier_suit_between_same_parties_seeks_: An earlier suit between the same parties seeking the same partition relief remains pending.

issues.definition: When a later suit seeks partition relief already sought in a pending earlier suit between the same parties, the partition right may be left for determination in the pending suit.
